That said, the leap from “high proximity” to “unequivocally surpasses the Vice President” doesn’t fully hold up when you widen the lens of what “influence” means in a government context.

First, the Vice President’s role isn’t just advisory. It carries formal, institutional power: presiding over the Senate, casting tie-breaking votes, participating in National Security Council processes, and serving as a constitutionally designated successor. Pence also had his own staff, policy portfolio, and relationships with Congress and party leadership. That gives him leverage that operates independently of proximity.

Second, influence isn’t only about who is in the room—it’s also about who can translate preferences into action across the system. A Vice President can coordinate agencies, negotiate with lawmakers, and mobilize political coalitions. An informal advisor, even a very trusted one, typically depends on others to implement ideas.

Third, proximity can be variable and context-dependent. Access might be high on some issues (for example, areas Ivanka focused on like workforce development), but limited in others, especially those dominated by formal national security or legislative processes where established roles carry more weight.

So a more defensible conclusion would be: Ivanka Trump likely had significant informal influence due to personal trust and access, sometimes rivaling or even exceeding that of formal officials in specific contexts. But saying she “unequivocally surpassed” the Vice President across the board overlooks the structural and institutional power that comes with Pence’s role.

In short, you’re right to emphasize proximity as a real source of influence—but it’s one variable among several, and not always the decisive one.
